The '''2000–01 Scottish Premier League''' (known as the '''2000–01 [[Bank of Scotland]] Premier League''' for sponsorship reasons) was the third season of the [[Scottish Premier League]], the top level of [[Association football|football]] in Scotland. It began on 29 July 2000 and concluded on 20 May 2001.

[[Rangers F.C.|Rangers]] were the defending champions.

[[Celtic F.C.|Celtic]] finished the season as league champions by a 15-point margin over Rangers, also winning both of the domestic cups to complete a [[Treble (association football)|domestic treble]], in their first season under the management of [[Martin O'Neill]].

==Changes from 1999–2000 season==
2000–01 saw the Scottish Premier League (SPL) expanded from 10 to 12 clubs, which was part of the agreement reached between the clubs in the SPL and the [[Scottish Football League]] when the top-tier clubs broke away in 1998.<ref name="Season review">{{cite news|url=https://spfl.co.uk/news/article/season-review-200001-2008-06-01/|publisher=[[Scottish Professional Football League]]|title=Season review 2000/01|access-date=6 February 2018|archive-date=2 July 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180702233302/https://spfl.co.uk/news/article/season-review-200001-2008-06-01/|url-status=live}}</ref>

With the expansion of the league, the league 'split' was introduced to avoid the need for clubs to play 44 fixtures in a season,<ref name="44 fixtures">{{cite news |last=Mullaney |first=Paul |date=8 April 2013 |title=Scottish Premier League: In Defence of the Split |website=[[Bleacher Report]] |url=https://bleacherreport.com/articles/1596665-scottish-premier-league-in-defence-of-the-split |url-status=live |access-date=6 February 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180604105757/http://bleacherreport.com/articles/1596665-scottish-premier-league-in-defence-of-the-split |archive-date=4 June 2018}}</ref> which would be the case if the quadruple round-robin format of the previous season was followed. Instead, after 33 rounds of matches, by which time all clubs had played each other three times, the league split into a 'top six' and 'bottom six' with clubs only competing against teams within their own section for the final five fixtures. Points achieved during the first phase of 33 matches were carried forward to the second phase but after the first phase was completed, clubs cannot move out of their own section in the league, even if they achieved more or fewer points than a higher or lower ranked team, respectively.<ref name="Split explanation">{{cite news|url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/sport1/hi/football/scot_prem/1251646.stm|title=Guide to the SPL split|date=31 March 2001|publisher=[[BBC Sport]]|access-date=6 February 2001|archive-date=4 September 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170904120433/http://news.bbc.co.uk/sport1/hi/football/scot_prem/1251646.stm|url-status=live}}</ref> The new format received widespread criticism from SPL managers.<ref name="Fear factor worries McLeish">{{cite news|url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/sport1/hi/football/teams/h/hibernian/825790.stm|publisher=[[BBC Sport]]|title=Fear factor worries McLeish|date=9 July 2000|access-date=24 April 2008}}</ref>

Results in European competition over the previous five years saw the league move up from 21st to 15th in the [[UEFA coefficient#Men's Association coefficient|UEFA country coefficient]] ranking. This meant that the league was granted an additional berth in the [[UEFA Champions League]] qualifying rounds for the following season.<ref name="UEFA country ranking">{{cite news|url=https://kassiesa.home.xs4all.nl/bert/uefa/history/qual2001.html|publisher=Bert Kassies|title=Qualification for European club football 2001/02|access-date=6 February 2018|archive-date=16 August 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180816121331/http://kassiesa.home.xs4all.nl/bert/uefa/history/qual2001.html|url-status=live}}</ref>

==Teams==
Twelve clubs competed in the league, all of the participants in the [[1999–2000 Scottish Premier League]] and the top two clubs in the [[1999–2000 Scottish First Division]]. A play-off was due to take place between the bottom club of the Premier League ([[Aberdeen F.C.|Aberdeen]]) and the second- and third-placed club of the First Division ([[Dunfermline Athletic F.C.|Dunfermline Athletic]] and [[Falkirk F.C.|Falkirk]], respectively), but as Falkirk's stadium did not meet the minimum SPL seating requirements, this play-off did not take place, and Aberdeen and Dunfermline were automatically placed in the Premier League.<ref name="Play-off">{{cite news|url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/sport1/hi/football/teams/f/falkirk/1058414.stm|publisher=[[BBC News]]|title=Falkirk stadium hopes boost|date=6 December 2000|access-date=6 February 2018|archive-date=5 April 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200405042733/http://news.bbc.co.uk/sport1/hi/football/teams/f/falkirk/1058414.stm|url-status=live}}</ref>

[[St Mirren F.C.|St Mirren]] were promoted to the league as champions of the 1999–2000 First Division, securing the championship on 29 April 2000 with a 3–0 victory over [[Raith Rovers F.C.|Raith Rovers]] at [[Love Street (stadium)|Love Street]]. This was to be their first season at the top level of [[Football in Scotland|Scottish football]] since [[1991–92 Scottish Premier Division|1991–92]].

==Overview==
The 2000–01 title was won by [[Celtic F.C.|Celtic]] – their first SPL title, and their first Scottish title since winning the [[1997–98 Scottish Premier Division|1997–98 Premier Division]] – in [[Martin O'Neill]]'s first season as manager of the club. Celtic also went on to win the [[2000–01 Scottish Cup]] and the [[2000–01 Scottish League Cup]], completing a [[Treble (association football)|domestic treble]].<ref name="Season review"/> [[Henrik Larsson]] won the 2000–01 [[European Golden Shoe]] for his goalscoring, scoring 35 league goals and 53 goals in all competitions over the course of the season. The 35 goals Larsson scored in the league this season was a Scottish Premier League record.

Defending champions [[Rangers F.C.|Rangers]] finished second, 15 points behind their [[Old Firm]]-rivals. Celtic secured their title on 7 April 2001, with a 1–0 victory over [[St Mirren F.C.|St Mirren]] at [[Celtic Park]].<ref name="Celtic secure title">{{cite news|url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/sport1/hi/football/scot_prem/1265666.stm|title=Celtic recapture league title|date=7 April 2001|publisher=[[BBC News]]|access-date=6 February 2018|archive-date=16 October 2006|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20061016181312/http://news.bbc.co.uk/sport1/hi/football/scot_prem/1265666.stm|url-status=live}}</ref> The aforementioned match had the highest attendance of any match in SPL history. As champions, Celtic qualified for the [[UEFA Champions League|Champions League]], as did second-placed Rangers. Third-placed [[Hibernian F.C.|Hibernian]] and fourth-placed [[Kilmarnock F.C.|Kilmarnock]] qualified for the [[UEFA Cup]], while [[Dundee F.C.|Dundee]] became the first SPL club – and the first Scottish club since [[Partick Thistle F.C.|Partick Thistle]] in [[1995 UEFA Intertoto Cup|1995]] – to qualify for the [[UEFA Intertoto Cup]].

The record for the highest transfer fee ever paid by a Scottish club was broken twice over the course of the season. Firstly, by [[Chris Sutton]]'s transfer from [[Chelsea F.C.|Chelsea]] to Celtic on 10 July 2000 for £6&nbsp;million.<ref name="Sutton signing">{{cite news|url=https://www.theguardian.com/football/2000/jul/10/newsstory.sport2|title=Celtic to break bank for Sutton|work=[[The Guardian]]|date=10 July 2000|access-date=6 February 2018|archive-date=7 February 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180207062905/https://www.theguardian.com/football/2000/jul/10/newsstory.sport2|url-status=live}}</ref> Then, on 23 November 2000, the £12&nbsp;million fee paid by Rangers to [[Chelsea F.C.|Chelsea]] for [[Tore André Flo]] became the highest transfer fee ever paid by a Scottish club,<ref name="Flo signing">{{cite news|url=https://www.theguardian.com/football/2000/nov/23/newsstory.sport1|title=Flo completes £12m Rangers move|work=[[The Guardian]]|date=23 November 2000|access-date=6 February 2018}}</ref> and is a record which still stands as of 2025.<ref name="Season review"/> The signing of [[Claudio Caniggia]] for [[Dundee F.C.|Dundee]] in October 2000 was also seen by many as a major coup for the club,<ref name="Caniggia signing">{{cite news|url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/sport/4773017/Dundee-delight-as-Caniggia-signs.html|work=[[The Daily Telegraph]]|date=5 October 2000|title=Dundee delight as Caniggia signs|access-date=6 February 2018|archive-date=7 February 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180207122406/http://www.telegraph.co.uk/sport/4773017/Dundee-delight-as-Caniggia-signs.html|url-status=live}}</ref> and was just one of many signings of international players made under the management of [[Ivano Bonetti]].

St Mirren were relegated in what was their debut season in the SPL and their first appearance in Scotland's top division since [[1991–92 in Scottish football|1991–92]]. Their relegation was mathematically confirmed on the final day of the season with a 3–3 draw against [[Motherwell F.C.|Motherwell]], leaving them five points below 11th-placed [[Dundee United F.C.|Dundee United]].<ref name="Season review"/>
